idiom_name: function-table visitor with a capability probe (COM-style QueryInterface)
implementation_notes: C has neither classes nor virtual functions, so the extensible visitor is built from two hand-written pieces: an element struct that reaches the operation through a table of function pointers, and a visitor struct whose first member is a pointer to a const table of handlers - a default handler plus one slot per element kind it knows. Adding an element kind means adding a slot to a new visitor table, and the element asks whether the visitor it was handed carries that slot (`v->ops->size > 2`) before calling it, otherwise it falls back to the default handler; that negotiation is exactly what COM does with IUnknown::QueryInterface, where an old object answers 'no' for an interface invented after it shipped. Extending an existing visitor means copying its table and overwriting entries, C's way of inheriting an implementation. The classic form is worth its cost only when both the element set and the operation set evolve in shipped binaries, as in COM or kernel operation tables; for a closed element set a tagged struct plus a switch with a default arm is smaller, faster and checked by the compiler.
pitfalls: Inheriting a visitor means copying its operation table and overwriting slots: a copy that forgets the base slots, or the size marker the probe reads, either calls through a null pointer or silently loses the inherited handlers.

Viewing an element through its base pointer works only because the base struct is the first member; keep the accept table first and never compare or cast between element pointers that do not share that layout.
Nothing checks that the slot a new element probes and the slot a new visitor fills agree - keep the probe and the table layout in one header, or the two sides drift silently.
